$$

$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ \frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(1,1).$
worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ \frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =0, & \,\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}], & \,\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈0+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ y-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ y-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ y-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & ≈0+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 1-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 1-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 1-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}] \\  & =0+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 1-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-(1-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ -(1-\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2} \\  & =-{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

feedback.problem:

- Distributor $3$ gets $41%$ of the copies, and $95%$ of those copies are sold.

If $3%$ of all copies have some printing defect, $70%$ of defective copies are sold, and $2.5%$ of sold copies are defective, what is the probability that a randomly chosen copy bought by distributor $1$ is sold? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the event that a copy has a printing defect, $S$ be the event that a copy is sold, and ${D}_{1},{D}_{2},{D}_{3}$ be the event that a copy is given to distributor $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively.

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({D}_{1})=0.36 \\  & P({D}_{2})=0.23 &  & P(S|{D}_{2})=0.92 \\  & P({D}_{3})=0.41 &  & P(S|{D}_{3})=0.95\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${D}_{1}⊔{D}_{2}⊔{D}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({D}_{1})+P({D}_{2})+P({D}_{3})=0.36+0.23+0.41=1.
$$

- Since $3%$ of all copies has some printing defect, we have

$$
P(R)=0.03.
$$

- Since $70%$ of defective copies are sold, we have

$$
P(S|R)=0.7.
$$

- Since $2.5%$ of sold copies are defective, we have

$$
P(R|S)=0.025.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen copy bought by distributor $1$ is sold, which is represented as $P(S|{D}_{1}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R|S) & =\frac{P(S|R)P(R)}{P(S)} \\ P(R|S) & =\frac{P(S|R)P(R)}{P(S|{D}_{1})P({D}_{1})+P(S|{D}_{2})P({D}_{2})+P(S|{D}_{3})P({D}_{3})} \\ 0.025 & =\frac{(0.7)(0.03)}{P(S|{D}_{1})(0.36)+(0.92)(0.23)+(0.95)(0.41)} \\ 0.025 & =\frac{0.021}{0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(S|{D}_{1}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.025(0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011) & =0.021 \\ 0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011 & =\frac{0.021}{0.025} \\ 0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011 & =\frac{21}{25} \\ 0.36P(S|{D}_{1}) & =\frac{21}{25}-0.6011 \\ P(S|{D}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{0.36}(\frac{21}{25}-0.6011) \\ P(S|{D}_{1}) & ≈0.664\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force attracting two objects is proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers of mass:

$$
F=G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

where

- $F$ is the gravitational force between the objects, measured in Newtons $(\text{N}),$

- $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2})$ is the Newtonian constant of gravitation,

- ${m}_{1}$ and ${m}_{2}$ are the masses of the objects, measured in $\text{kg},$ and

- $r$ is the distance between their centers of mass, measured in $\text{m}.$

First, let's rearrange the formula to make $r$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{F} \\ r & =\sqrt{G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{F}}\end{aligned}
$$

Choosing ${m}_{1}=(4.5\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg}$ and ${m}_{2}=(2.8\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg}$ and substituting in the other known values, we have

$$

$$

Finally, taking the square root, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{23.345\times {10}^{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{23.345}\times \sqrt{{10}^{4}} \\  & =(4.8316…)\times {10}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounded to two significant figures, the distance between the two objects is
$(\,4.8\times {10}^{2}\,)\,\text{m}.$

feedback.problem: Three baskets, $A,B,$ and $C,$ contain pears. It is known that $\frac{1}{6}$ of the pears from basket $A$ and $\frac{1}{5}$ of those from basket $B$ are ripe. A basket is selected at random, and a pear is chosen at random from the basket. If the probability that the selected pear is ripe is $\frac{1}{4},$  what proportion of the pears from basket $C$ are ripe?
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the event that the pear is ripe, and

- let $A$ be the event that the pear comes from basket $A,$

- let $B$ be the event that the pear comes from basket $B,$

- let $C$ be the event that the pear comes from basket $C.$

Then the disjoint union $A⊔B⊔C$ covers the entire sample space.

To calculate the probability of selecting a ripe pear, we can use the law of total probability: 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R) & =P(R\cap A)+P(R\cap B)+P(R\cap C) \\  & =P(R|A)P(A)+P(R|B)P(B)+P(R|C)P(C)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each piece of information into mathematical notation.

- Since a basket is selected at random, we have

$$
P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

- Since the probability of picking a ripe pear from baskets $A$ and $B$ are $\frac{1}{6}$ and $\frac{1}{5},$ respectively, we have

$$
P(R|A)=\frac{1}{6},\,P(R|B)=\frac{1}{5}
$$

- Since the probability of picking a ripe pear from one of the baskets is $\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
P(R)=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability and solving for $P(R|C),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R) & =P(R|A)P(A)+P(R|B)P(B)+P(R|C)P(C) \\ \frac{1}{4} & =(\frac{1}{6})(\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{1}{5})(\frac{1}{3})+P(R|C)(\frac{1}{3}) \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{18}+\frac{1}{15}+\frac{1}{3}\cdot P(R|C) \\ \frac{1}{3}\cdot P(R|C) & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{18}-\frac{1}{15} \\ \frac{1}{3}\cdot P(R|C) & =\frac{23}{180} \\ P(R|C) & =\frac{23}{60}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{23}{60}$ of the pears from basket $C$ are ripe.

feedback.problem: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves $xy=C,$ where $C$ and $K$ are parameters.
feedback.worked_solution:
Orthogonal trajectories are families of curves that intersect another given family of curves at right angles. In other words, the tangent lines of curves from each family are perpendicular at every intersection point.

Let's determine the slope of the family of curves given by $xy=C.$ First, we implicitly differentiate with respect to $x$ and solve for the derivative of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(xy) & =\frac{d}{dx}(C) \\ y+x{y}^{′} & =0 \\ x{y}^{′} & =-y \\ {y}^{′} & =-\frac{y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the parameter $C$ has already been eliminated.

For a curve to intersect this family orthogonally, its slope ${y}_{⊥}^{′}$ must be the negative reciprocal of the slope ${y}^{′}$ above. Hence,

$$
{y}_{⊥}^{′}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{′}}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{y}{x})}=\frac{x}{y}.
$$

Hence, the orthogonal trajectories must satisfy

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x}{y}.
$$

To find the general solution, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y\cdot \frac{dy}{dx} & =x \\ \int y\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}\,dx & =\int x\,dx \\ \int y\,dy & =\int x\,dx \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{K}_{1} \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+K\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K=2{K}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Therefore, the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves $xy=C,$ where $C$ is a parameter, are given by

$$
{y}^{2}={x}^{2}+K,
$$

where $K$ is a parameter. Some curves from each family for specific parameter values are given in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070542/assets/98159dfb60fd280468ad8165475b5ba58e41658174a932b4c9555ef1153a577c.png)

**Note**: For the slopes ${y}^{′}$ and ${y}_{⊥}^{′},$ we divide by $x$ and $y,$ respectively. So, the orthogonal trajectories are only defined on the region $x,y\ne 0.$

feedback.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation.

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}={y}^{2}-y
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution* $z={y}^{-1}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}-\frac{1}{z} \\ -\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-z\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-1+z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-1,\,Q(x)=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-x}$ yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x}\cdot (\frac{dz}{dx}-z) & ={e}^{-x}\cdot (-1) \\ {e}^{-x}\frac{dz}{dx}-{e}^{-x}z & =-{e}^{-x} \\ \frac{d}{dx}(z{e}^{-x}) & =-{e}^{-x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(z{e}^{-x})\,dx\, & =-\int {e}^{-x}\,dx \\ z{e}^{-x} & ={e}^{-x}+C \\ z & =1+C{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =1+C{e}^{x} \\ y & =\frac{1}{1+C{e}^{x}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
For which of the following functions is it valid to differentiate under the integral sign?

- ${F}_{1}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+tx)}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (-1,1)$
- ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{x-t}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (1,2)$
- ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{|x-t|}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+tx)}{1+{x}^{2}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (-1,1)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(-1,1)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R$ (since $1+tx>0$). Computing the  partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=\frac{x}{(1+tx)(1+{x}^{2})}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (-1,1).$

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{1}{x-t}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (1,2)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(1,2)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=\frac{1}{(x-t)^{2}},
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (1,2).$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|x-t|}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,1)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that this function is undefined when $x=t,$ since the denominator vanishes. Thus, ${f}_{3}$ is not continuous on $R,$ and differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

feedback.problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}{y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0
$$

Let ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ be solutions to the second-order homogeneous differential equation above, where $Q(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ The Wronskian satisfies $W(0)=2.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.
The Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies the following first-order differential equation:

$$
{W}^{′}(x)={{field-1}}W(x)
$$

Solving this equation, we get

$$
W={{field-2}}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Now, using the fact that $W(0)=2,$ we obtain 
{{field-3}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{e}^{-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)} \\ W & =C{e}^{-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(0)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(0) & =C{e}^{-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)} \\ 2 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $W(x)\ne 0\text{ for all }x\in R.$

feedback.problem:
Consider a linear transformation $T$ that maps ${R}^{2}$ onto  ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $\text{Im}(T)={0}$
- $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$
- $\text{nullity}(T)=1$, where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear transformation $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto  ${R}^{2}$ if and only if 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=2
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. The condition $\text{rank}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to

$$
\text{Im}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=0$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={0}.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have that 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

**Step 1**: Find the equilibrium solutions of the differential equation.

Therefore, the equilibrium solutions are $y=-2$ and $y=1.$

**Step 2**: Find the intervals of $y$ for which $f(y)>0$ and $f(y)<0.$

feedback.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(4-x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070542/assets/d4e5b78932f8ff6155ac81e12538eb31ac211c9d27d6a2b0c67542527ccd3b2a.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(4-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4-x & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=4\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $6$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2>0$ | $0$ | $-2<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=4\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (4-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =4(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+18 \\ {v}^{2} & =8x-{x}^{2}+36 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(4)=\sqrt{-(4)^{2}+8(4)+36}=2\sqrt{13}\,m/s
$$

feedback.problem:
The volume $X(t)$ (in $\text{L}$) of water in a container as it fills toward its maximum capacity can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dX}{dt}=0.4(3-X),
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial volume is $1.5\,\text{L},$ how long does it take for the container to reach a volume of $2\,\text{L}?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer.
feedback.worked_solution:
We're told that the container's volume is modeled by the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dX}{dt}=0.4(3-X).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dX}{3-X} & =0.4\,dt \\ \int \frac{dX}{3-X} & =\int 0.4\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-X| & =0.4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $3-X>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$
Next, we solve for $X(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-X & ={e}^{-0.4t-C} \\ 3-X & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-0.4t} \\ 3-X & =K{e}^{-0.4t} \\ X & =3-K{e}^{-0.4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial volume was $1.5\,\text{L}.$ So, we apply the initial condition $X(0)=1.5,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1.5 & =3-K{e}^{0} \\ 1.5 & =3-K \\ K & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
X(t)=3-1.5{e}^{-0.4t}.
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the volume is $2\,\text{L}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}X({t}_{1}) & =2 \\ 3-1.5{e}^{-0.4{t}_{1}} & =2 \\ 1 & =1.5{e}^{-0.4{t}_{1}} \\ {e}^{-0.4{t}_{1}} & =\frac{2}{3} \\ -0.4{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{0.4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =1.013… \\  & ≈1\,\text{minute},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

feedback.problem:
If $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A+8I)=2,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $A+8I$ is singular
- $\lambda =-8$ is an eigenvalue of $A$
- $\text{rank}(A+8I)=2$
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a $3\times 3$ matrix $M,$ we have the following by the invertible matrix theorem:

$M$ is invertible $\,⇔\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(M)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(M))=3=\text{rank}(M) \\  & \text{Null}(M)={0} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(M))=0=\text{nullity}(M)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $M$ has $3$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(M)+\text{nullity}(M)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statements I is true. By the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A+8I)\ne 0,$ we obtain that $A+8I$ must be singular.

- Statement II is true. Notice that if $M=A+8I$ is singular, then $(A+8I)x=0$ has nonzero solutions which will be eigenvectors of $A.$ As a result, $\lambda =-8$ is an eigenvalue of $A.$

- Statement III is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A+8I) & =3-\text{nullity}(A+8I) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

feedback.problem:
The population $y(t)$ of Weddell seals in a certain region of Antarctica follows the logistic growth model

$$
{y}^{′}=1.2y-0.002{y}^{2},\,y(0)=100,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in years. According to this model, what is the maximum possible seal population?
feedback.worked_solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity. 

The carrying capacity $a$ represents the maximum possible population. A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070542/assets/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =1.2y-0.002{y}^{2} \\  & =0.002y(600-y)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=600.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $600,$ and we conclude that the number of seals cannot exceed $600.$

feedback.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $G$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $G,$ then $G$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $G=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $G,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
G={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}G & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 & 9 \\ -30 & 17\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -2 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-3\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=-3\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(5)(5)}{(1+3\text{i})(1-3\text{i})}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le x-2}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x-2\,⟹\,x=y+2
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
x=4.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y-2\le x\le 4},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070542/assets/575e7e482f88635f6267405f66857a5488dac79833fce16d3d998df19e24d119.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{x-2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y+2}^{4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨-1,0,x{y}^{3}⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=yz.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨3x{y}^{2},-{y}^{3},0⟩,\,∇f=⟨0,z,y⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(0,-1,2).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & z & y \\ -1 & 0 & x{y}^{3}\end{aligned}| \\  & =[z(x{y}^{3})-y(0)]i-[0(x{y}^{3})-y(-1)]j+[0(0)-z(-1)]k \\  & =xz{y}^{3}\,i-y\,j+z\,k \\  & =⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =yz⟨3x{y}^{2},-{y}^{3},0⟩+⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3xz{y}^{3},-z{y}^{4},0⟩+⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨4xz{y}^{3},-z{y}^{4}-y,z⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(0,-1,2) & =⟨4(0)(2)(-1)^{3},-2(-1)^{4}-(-1),2⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
